title: Number, quantity, degree and intensity
subtitle: a vast amount, loads of, utterly ridiculous
summary: Learn the adjectives that grade number and quantity from minute to vast, the informal words like loads and tons, and the intensifiers utter, total and wholly with the words they go with.

lesson.heading: Number or amount?
lesson.text: Use **number** with countable nouns and **amount** with uncountable nouns. This is one of the commonest slips at this level, so check the noun before you choose.

examples.text: A vast **quantity** of sand was blown on to the road.

lesson.heading: Adjectives of number and quantity, smallest to biggest
rows: rather formal; the stress is on the second syllable
the emphasis is on being noticeable
vast is often used with quantity and amounts

lesson.heading: These adjectives in use
lesson.text: Notice which noun each adjective is used with. *Minute* and *tiny* go with amounts; *considerable* and *significant* go happily with number; *excessive* always suggests that there is too much of something.

examples.text: Even **minute** amounts of toxic material can be dangerous.
Add just a **tiny** amount of chilli pepper, or else it may get too hot.
A **considerable** number of people failed to get tickets.
A **significant** number of students have dropped out of university in the last year.
There is an **excessive** amount of sugar in many soft drinks.

lesson.heading: Informal words for number and quantity
rows: a dozen is 12; dozens of means many, especially with countables
a score is 20 or about 20; scores of means a large number of; usually formal
informal; countable or uncountable; usually with singular there is
informal; especially for things, not often for abstract nouns
a tiny amount of any liquid
lesson.note: The verb agrees with the noun that follows, not with tons or loads: There was tons of food. / There are tons of apples on this tree.

lesson.heading: Informal quantity words in use
lesson.text: These words are very common in speech. Note the singular verb in *There's loads of time* - it follows the uncountable noun *time*.

examples.text: I've got **dozens of** nails in my tool box.
**Scores of** people were injured when the gas tank exploded.
There's **loads of** time yet, slow down!
There was absolutely **tons of** food at the party - far too much.
Just a **drop of** milk for me, please.

lesson.heading: Utter, total and wholly - collocations
rows: nonsense, contempt, silence, confusion, chaos, despair
There was utter chaos during the transport strike.
I was utterly confused by the instruction manual.
She looked at him in total disbelief.
The two brothers have totally different personalities.
The success of the project was wholly dependent on the weather.
lesson.note: Utter(ly), total(ly) and wholly all mean complete(ly), but each one keeps its own set of partners.

lesson.text: Utter goes with 'strong' nouns - chaos, nonsense, despair - so you will never hear *utter happiness* or *utter comfort*.

exercises.prompt: It takes a ___ amount of time to learn to ski well.
exercises.explanation: Considerable is a formal word for a large amount.

exercises.prompt: The scientists found only a ___ amount of the chemical in the food and said it was safe to eat.
exercises.explanation: Minute is the formal word for an extremely small amount.

exercises.prompt: ___ amounts of money are wasted by government departments every year.
exercises.explanation: Vast means extremely large and goes well with amounts of money.

exercises.prompt: An ___ amount of fat in your diet is dangerous.
exercises.explanation: Excessive means too much and is always negative.

exercises.prompt: Last year we didn't really notice an increase in prices, but this year the increase has been ___.
exercises.explanation: Significant means noticeably large - the point here is that the difference was noticeable.

exercises.prompt: Which word is correct? '___ of people came on to the streets to hear his speech.'
exercises.explanation: Scores of means a large number of people; bags and loads are used for amounts, not for crowds in this pattern.

exercises.prompt: We've got ___ of time. The train doesn't leave till 2.30.
exercises.explanation: Loads, heaps and bags of all work with uncountable time; dozens and scores do not.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct verb: 'There ___ tons of food left over after the dinner party.'
exercises.explanation: The verb follows the noun after tons of - food is uncountable, so the verb is singular.

exercises.prompt: Which intensifier does each word normally go with?
You thought someone's behaviour was completely unacceptable: 'His behaviour was ___ unacceptable.'
exercises.explanation: Wholly collocates with dependent, inadequate and unacceptable.

exercises.prompt: You listened to someone's story and did not believe a word of it: 'I listened to the story in ___ disbelief.'
exercises.explanation: Total collocates most often with disbelief and ban.

exercises.statement: We should say 'a large number of money'.
exercises.explanation: Money is uncountable, so it must be a large amount of money.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to say that a way of working produced complete chaos.
exercises.answer: That way of working produced utter chaos.
exercises.explanation: Utter combines with strong nouns such as chaos, nonsense and despair.
